transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. What brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Well... I guess what brings me in is that I just keep dodging anything that even smells like that old job. Office buildings, security talks, those networking events near the work sites... 

I actually used to run a lot of those events when I was the operations manager. You wouldn't believe the logistics involved just to get fifty people in a room with decent coffee. We used this one caterer who always brought those little cucumber finger sandwiches, but they'd get completely soggy if you didn't time the delivery exactly right. Managing vendors is practically a full-time job on its own. 

But anyway, now? I won't go near any of it. And if I do happen to run into someone and they start asking about the day it happened, I just make some excuse and get out of there. I'll tell them I have to go call my sister—she's out in Florida right now, actually, dealing with all that awful humidity, which I could never stand. But yeah, I just make my excuse and leave. I just can't be around it.
Can you tell me more about the day you're referring to? Do you find yourself re-experiencing what happened, like through bad memories, nightmares, or feeling like it’s happening all over again?

Well, the day it happened... it was just a regular Tuesday, or maybe Wednesday? No, Tuesday, because they always did the trash pickup on Tuesdays, and I remember complaining to the building super about the smell near the loading dock. He was this grumpy guy, Frank, who always wore these terrible neon orange suspenders. I don't know where he even found them. 

But, um, about what you asked—the memories. Yeah. It's like... out of nowhere I'll just be washing dishes, or I'll be driving past a warehouse gate, and suddenly the whole scene just pops right back into my head. It's so sharp. I can actually hear the panic in people's voices all over again, and my chest gets so tight, just like I'm right back there in the middle of it. 

Which is awful, because I used to love driving. My husband and I used to take these long road trips out to the coast in his old Buick. It had those plush velour seats, you know? They don't make cars like that anymore, everything is so plastic now. But yeah, the memories just hit me out of the blue, and it feels like it's happening right then and there.
Do you find yourself avoiding certain places, people, or activities because they remind you of the event?

Well, I did mention I avoid the office buildings and the networking events, right? I just can't do it. But other places... I don't know, I haven't really noticed avoiding anything else specific. I mean, I still go to the grocery store and the dry cleaners. Though I did switch dry cleaners recently because the one on Elm Street kept losing my husband's shirts. Can you believe that? Three shirts in one month. Good shirts, too, the cotton ones he got from that outlet mall up in Maine. We went there for our anniversary a couple years ago. The lobster rolls up there are just incredible, they use so much butter on the bun... but anyway, no, besides the work stuff, I don't think I avoid much else.
Have you noticed any changes in the way you feel or think about yourself or the world since the event happened?

Well, I guess... yeah, things do feel different now. Since that day, I just catch myself thinking that nobody is really safe to trust. I mean, even someone you managed, someone you actually tried to help out, can just turn around and become dangerous. It really makes you second-guess everyone. 

Which reminds me of this girl I used to manage, Sarah. I spent weeks training her on the new inventory software. It was this clunky system, practically ancient, and it took forever just to generate a simple report. You had to click through like five different screens just to see the stock levels. But anyway, I spent all this time helping her, and then she ended up taking credit for my quarterly analysis at the big regional meeting. Can you believe that? Just stood right up there and acted like she ran all the numbers herself. I even bought her a coffee that morning from the place down the street—the one that makes those amazing blueberry muffins with the sugar crystals on top. They always sell out by 9 AM, so you have to get there early. But yeah, people just... they really surprise you, you know? You just can't trust anyone to be safe anymore.
Have you noticed yourself feeling more fearful, angry, or on edge since the event happened?

Well, I do feel on edge, yes. And angry. Oh, I get so angry lately. It's like the littlest things just set me off completely. Like the other day, my niece came over and she left the front door unlocked. I just snapped at her, yelled way louder than I meant to, and then I felt so ashamed about it afterward. 

But honestly, she's always been a bit scatterbrained. Even when she was little, she would leave her toys all over the driveway. I remember stepping on this hard plastic dinosaur she had—a green one, a triceratops, I think? It hurt so badly I thought I broke my toe. We had to put ice on it for an hour. And my sister, her mother, she never really disciplined her. She read all those parenting books that tell you to just let kids express themselves, which I think is just an excuse not to parent. My sister and I never really saw eye to eye on that. She always thought I was too strict. But anyway, yes, I get irritated so easily now. If someone interrupts me when I'm talking, I just bite their head off. It's not like me, but I just can't seem to stop it.
Do you find yourself being easily startled or constantly on guard, like you're always watching for danger?

Yes, actually. I'm always watching everything now. Whenever I walk into a meeting room or a restaurant, the very first thing I do is look for the exits. I have to know where they are. And I watch people's hands, just to see what they're doing. I always have to pick a seat where my back is to the wall, so nobody can come up behind me. 

It's funny, because my husband hates when I do that at restaurants. We used to have this favorite Italian place downtown, Luigi's. Oh, they had the most incredible eggplant parmesan. The sauce was so rich, they simmered it all day, and they'd serve it with this crusty garlic bread that was always warm when they brought it to the table. We used to go there every Friday night, but then they changed ownership a few years ago and the new chef completely ruined the menu. He started putting kale in the minestrone soup. Can you imagine? Kale. It was just awful. We haven't been back since. But anyway, yes, I'm always on guard now. I just can't relax unless I know exactly what's going on around me.
Since the event, have you noticed that you often feel things like guilt, shame, or an inability to experience positive emotions like joy or happiness?

Well, yes... it's like the joy is just gone. I try, I really do. I used to love putting on salsa music while I was painting or cooking Sunday dinner. Those things used to lift me right up, you know? But now, I just go through the motions and that good feeling... it just doesn't come the way it used to. 

Speaking of Sunday dinners, I used to make this pot roast that took four hours to cook. You had to sear the chuck roast first—get a really good crust on it in a cast iron skillet—and then slow-braise it with carrots and pearl onions. My grandmother taught me how to make it when I was just a teenager. She was such a wonderful cook, but she never measured anything. She just threw a handful of flour here, a pinch of salt there. It drove me crazy when I was trying to write down her recipes. I remember one time we were making her famous peach cobbler, and she told me to use "a glug" of vanilla extract. What is a glug? I still don't know! I ended up using way too much and the whole thing tasted like perfume. My grandfather ate it anyway, bless his heart. He would eat anything she put in front of him. But yeah, I still make the pot roast sometimes, but it just... I don't feel anything when I do it anymore. It's just a chore now.
Have these symptoms been causing you trouble in your daily life, like at work, in your relationships, or with activities you used to handle easily?

Well, yes, they have. It's actually been really hard at work. I'm an operations manager, so I'm used to being the one in charge, the one keeping everything running smoothly. But lately... I've actually turned down a few interviews for promotions. I just can't reliably get through meetings or site visits anymore without feeling like I need to shut down or just leave the room. 

Which is a shame, because I used to love site visits. I remember this one time, oh, it must have been five or six years ago, we went out to this new facility they were building out in Westlake. It was the middle of July, and it was so hot you could practically see the heat waves coming off the pavement. We had to wear these awful hard hats that just trapped all the heat right against your head. Anyway, the site foreman, his name was Gary, I think... or maybe Terry? No, it was Gary. He had this little terrier mix that he brought to the site every day. The dog wore a tiny little high-visibility vest! It was the cutest thing I've ever seen. But that dog was a menace. It kept stealing the workers' lunches. I actually saw it run off with a whole pastrami sandwich once. Gary had to buy lunch for the whole crew that day to make up for it. We ordered from this deli down the street that made the most incredible potato salad. It had dill in it, which I never thought I'd like, but it was actually really refreshing. 

But anyway, yeah, I just can't do things like that anymore. I've even stopped taking on volunteer responsibilities. And my family, and the mentoring circles I used to be so active in... they're noticing. I'm just less present. People have started asking me why I'm pulling back instead of leading like I always have. It's just... I can't do it right now.
How long have you been experiencing these symptoms since the event happened?

Well, it's been going on ever since I was fired after that armed incident... so, about a year and seven months ago. 

I still can't believe they let me go after all the years I gave that company. I started there right out of high school, you know. I was just a receptionist back then, answering phones on this massive switchboard that looked like something out of a 1950s movie. It had all these little flashing lights and cords you had to plug in. My supervisor back then was this woman named Brenda. Oh, Brenda was a character. She had this big, teased-up hair—like, Dolly Parton big—and she wore these bright blue eyeshadows that matched her outfits perfectly. She used to smoke right at her desk, which seems so crazy now! Can you imagine just lighting up a cigarette in an office today? But back then, everyone did it. She had this heavy crystal ashtray that she'd tap her long red fingernails against when she was thinking. She actually taught me how to type without looking at the keys. We had these old IBM Selectric typewriters... the ones with the little metal ball that spun around and smacked the paper. They were so loud, it sounded like a machine gun going off when you got typing really fast. 

But anyway, yes, it's been about a year and seven months since everything happened and they let me go.
